title: Hypothesis Testing
subtopics: Type I and Type II Errors
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of hypothesis testing and identify its main inputs, outputs or constraints.
Apply null and alternative hypotheses in a minimal example and state the expected result before checking it.
Test one relevant edge, missing or failure case and describe a limitation of the result.

content.intro: Hypothesis Testing is part of Probability, Statistical Inference, and Experiments. Start with null and alternative hypotheses and connect it to the worked example and expected result.
content.why_it_matters: A test result depends on the question, design, assumptions and uncertainty; it does not by itself measure importance.

content_blocks.title: Why this matters
content_blocks.text: A test result depends on the question, design, assumptions and uncertainty; it does not by itself measure importance. The example is intentionally small so you can predict its result before checking it in a local R session.

items.title: Null and Alternative Hypotheses
items.text: Compare null and alternative hypotheses using concrete trade-offs, assumptions and maintenance needs; state when each choice is appropriate.

items.title: Test Statistics
items.text: Explain test statistics in the context of hypothesis testing, connect it to the example, and verify one expected result or edge case.

items.title: P-Values
items.text: Explain p-values in the context of hypothesis testing, connect it to the example, and verify one expected result or edge case.

items.title: Significance Levels
items.text: Explain significance levels in the context of hypothesis testing, connect it to the example, and verify one expected result or edge case.

items.title: Type I and Type II Errors
items.text: For type i and type ii errors, include a failing or boundary case and explain how it should be detected without silently losing information.

items.title: Statistical Significance vs. Practical Importance
items.text: For statistical significance vs. practical importance, state the statistical question and assumptions first, then describe the estimate or diagnostic in context.

content_blocks.title: Work through it
content_blocks.text: State the null hypothesis, test assumptions, and write a conclusion in the study context. Change one input or condition at a time, compare the observed result with your prediction, and write down one limitation.

content_blocks.title: R example: Hypothesis Testing
content_blocks.code:
# Lesson 145: Hypothesis Testing
measurements <- c(7, 9, 11)
mean(measurements)

content_blocks.limitations: Treat this as a descriptive calculation; state the sample/design assumptions before making an inferential claim. Verify the snippet and expected output with the supported R and package versions before publishing.

content_blocks.title: Common pitfall
content_blocks.text: Do not treat a syntactically plausible example as proof of correctness. For hypothesis testing, check the input type, missing/empty cases, output shape, and domain assumptions.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a p-value, coefficient or score as a complete conclusion.
common_mistakes.why: Study design, assumptions, effect size and uncertainty shape interpretation.
common_mistakes.fix: State the question, inspect diagnostics and report uncertainty and limitations.

common_mistakes.problem: Using test data during feature selection or tuning.
common_mistakes.why: This leaks information and leads to an overly optimistic evaluation.
common_mistakes.fix: Separate training, validation and final test roles before modeling.

common_mistakes.problem: Reporting a model without comparing it with a baseline.
common_mistakes.why: Complexity does not guarantee useful performance.
common_mistakes.fix: Evaluate an appropriate simple baseline with task-relevant metrics.
